newsitem.title: FRANCE: Protest, far-right voters hold key to French poll.
newsitem.headline: Protest, far-right voters hold key to French poll.

text.p: Voters who abstained in protest or who backed the far right in the first round of France's parliamentary election hold the key to Sunday's cliffhanger runoff ballot.

Political commentators said Gaullist President Jacques Chirac could avoid "cohabitation", or power-sharing with a left-wing prime minister, only by winning over a large slice of those who deserted the ruling centre-right coalition when the Socialist-Communist bloc grabbed an upset victory a week ago.

Within the space of just a few days, Chirac has buried his unpopular Prime Minister Alain Juppe and fielded socially-conscious Philippe Seguin and free-marketeer Alain Madelin in a "dream ticket" attempt to salvage the coalition.

"The Seguin-Madelin ticket has come pretty late. It blurs the outlook because there has never been a change of leader (Prime Minister Alain Juppe) between the two rounds of an election," political commentator Pascal Perrineau said.

"The results of the first round show that the centre-right does have some reserves in the contingent which abstained. But that won't be enough. It must capture a majority of those who abstained and an important slice of voters who backed the far-right National Front," Perrineau told France-Info radio.

Centre-right leaders are openly betting on a favourable swing of far-right voters despite Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen, whose party took 15 percent of the vote, urging voters to "punish" the coalition.

Le Pen featured prominently in newspapers which pictured him -- eyes popping and mouth wide open as he yelled in rage -- thrusting towards a female Socialist candidate shortly before he threw her to the ground in a Paris suburb on Friday.

Across the country, 80 of the 577 constituencies are too close to call with less than two percentage points separating candidates in the first round, when the combined left polled 40.1 percent to 36.5 for the centre-right.
Socialist leader Lionel Jospin said on Friday: "I ask French men and women...to confirm and amplify the first-round vote."

The conservatives appealed to voters not to let "the trap slam shut" and think of the future rather than venting short-term irritation at record unemployment and austerity necessary to qualify France for a European single currency.
In an eve-of-poll protest, several thousand people marched through Paris to demand the repeal of the Maastricht Treaty on European unification.
The demonstration was called by the National Committee for the Repeal of the Maastricht Treaty, created by the far-left Workers Party and deputies from the Communist and Citizens Movement parties.

Popular newspaper France-Soir, following a lead set by other dailies, flouted a law banning the publishing of opinion polls in the week before elections. It printed six surveys and runs the risk of a 500,000 franc ($88,000) fine.
The anti-surveys law is meant to avoid swaying France's 38.5 million voters. The polls, or rumours of them, are a major factor moving the Paris stock market ahead of the election.
First projected results are due as soon as polls close on Sunday at 8 p.m. (1800 GMT).

Violence marred the eve of voting, with a bomb exploding outside a post office in the southern port city of Marseille overnight. Police said the bomb late on Friday night caused damage but no casualties.
The Historic Wing of the Corsican National Liberation Front claimed responsibility for the attack in a statement which also noted "the end of the Juppe era".
